name: B.9

origin.place: Michurinsk College of Horticulture (now Michurinsk State Agrarian University), Tambov region
origin.parentage: M.8 x 'Krasny Standart' (Red Standard), a red-fleshed Michurin apple
origin.note: Bred by V.I. Budagovsky and introduced in the late 1940s; the red leaves and red-tinged wood come from the red-fleshed parent.

support: Permanent stake or trellis for life; roots are brittle
soil_notes: needs fertile, weed-free, well-drained soil and irrigation in dry spells; copes with heavier soils better than M.26 because it resists collar rot
best_for: high-density spindles and trellised trees in cold-winter regions; hardy dwarfing interstem
avoid_when: dry unirrigated sites, poor or grassed ground, places where trees cannot be supported
variety_fit: Best with moderately vigorous scions; weak or spur-type varieties can be over-dwarfed unless soil and irrigation are good.
notes: Very winter-hardy red-leaved dwarfing stock from central Russia, a little smaller than M.9 in most trials and very precocious and yield-efficient. Leaves and young shoots blight readily when inoculated, but Cornell work found the mature rootstock shank highly resistant to rootstock blight in field plantings; it resists collar rot but is susceptible to woolly aphid and mildew. A European (trailing) and a North American (upright) strain circulate, the latter producing more burr knots; stoolbed propagation is difficult and the stock is drought-sensitive.

name: B.10

origin.place: Michurinsk State Agrarian University, Tambov region
origin.note: Michurinsk selection 62-396 (year of cross from the selection number), renamed B.10 for Western trials. One US extension page gives 'M.27 x Robusta 5', which conflicts with Michurinsk records and a 2023 SSR pedigree study.

support: Support advised in intensive plantings; anchorage reported better than M.9
soil_notes: treat like other M.9-class stocks: fertile, well-drained soil, weed control and irrigation
best_for: high-density orchards in cold-winter regions wanting M.9-sized trees with more hardiness
notes: Red-leaved Michurinsk selection 62-396, bred for winter hardiness and released in the West as B.10. In Pennsylvania and NC-140 trials it gave M.9-class trees, in one trial slightly smaller than M.9 T337, with yield efficiency at or above M.9 T337 and wide branch angles; in Polish trials (as B 396) trees matched M.9 EMLA in size and out-yielded it. Fire blight tolerance is reported but pest and disease data outside Russia are still thin.

name: B.118

origin.place: Michurinsk State Agrarian University, Tambov region
origin.parentage: B.9 x 13-14 per Michurinsk records; some Western sources give 'Moscow Pear' x mixed M.8/M.9 pollen
origin.note: Selection 54-118 (year of cross from the selection number); red-leaved.

support: Free-standing once established; stake for the first years
soil_notes: vigorous enough for weaker soils and replant ground; avoid waterlogged sites given mixed reports on Phytophthora
best_for: large free-standing trees in very cold regions; weak soils; hardy frame for interstem trees
avoid_when: small gardens or high-density plantings; wet, Phytophthora-prone ground
variety_fit: Gives big trees with vigorous scions; better suited to spur-type or weak varieties that need a strong root.
notes: Very winter-hardy Michurinsk stock giving trees roughly 70-90% of seedling size, between MM.106 and MM.111 depending on site. Free-standing, rarely suckers and roots well in stoolbeds, but crops later than MM.106. Reported moderately resistant to fire blight; collar rot reports conflict (tolerant to susceptible), and North American experience is limited.

name: B.490

origin.place: Michurinsk College of Horticulture (now Michurinsk State Agrarian University), Tambov region
origin.note: Selection 57-490 (year of cross from the selection number); red inner bark and red-tinged leaves.

support: Stake for the first years; support advisable on exposed sites
soil_notes: adaptable MM.106-class stock; collar-rot resistance makes it safer than MM.106 on heavier ground
best_for: medium-sized orchard or garden trees in cold regions; a hardier alternative to MM.106
avoid_when: where woolly aphid is a serious problem; small gardens needing dwarf trees
notes: Hardy Michurinsk stock in the MM.106 size class that crops early for its vigour. It roots readily from hardwood cuttings, rarely forms burr knots and seldom suckers. Moderately resistant to fire blight and collar rot but susceptible to woolly aphid; tested only to a limited extent in North America.

name: B.491

origin.place: Michurinsk College of Horticulture (now Michurinsk State Agrarian University), Tambov region
origin.parentage: B.9 x 13-14 (2023 SSR pedigree study); an earlier Michurinsk account lists B.9 x 'Naliv Aliy'
origin.note: Selection 57-491 (year of cross from the selection number); red leaves and pink wood.

support: Permanent stake or trellis; wood is brittle
soil_notes: needs fertile, well-drained, weed-free soil; keep away from wet ground (Phytophthora)
best_for: very small trees or hardy dwarfing interstems in severe-winter climates
avoid_when: fire-blight areas, wet soils, poor or grassed ground, commercial blocks wanting full-size dwarfs
variety_fit: Only vigorous scions make a useful tree; weak varieties are stunted.
notes: Very dwarfing, very winter-hardy Michurinsk stock in the M.27 class; in the NC-140 1994 Gala trial trees were about a third to a half the size of those on B.9, with slightly lower yield efficiency. Considered too dwarfing for most commercial orchards but useful as a hardy interstem, and it propagates easily in stoolbeds. Brittle, and very susceptible to fire blight and Phytophthora.

name: B.64-194

origin.place: Michurinsk State Agrarian University, Tambov region
origin.note: Michurinsk selection classed as semi-dwarfing in Russian sources (year of cross from the selection number); licensed for testing in France and the USA as a donor of frost resistance.

best_for: breeding and trial use; cold-climate semi-dwarf trials
notes: Semi-dwarfing selection from the Michurinsk (Budagovsky) programme that was passed to French and US institutions for evaluation and breeding. Unlike B.9, B.10 or B.118 it has little published orchard data in English, so its vigour, disease reactions and hardiness rating are not well established.

name: P.1

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice
origin.note: From S.W. Zagaja's winter-hardiness breeding programme; one of the first P-series introductions.

best_for: hardy semi-dwarf trees in cold continental climates (historical/trial interest)
notes: Early Polish M.9 x Antonovka selection that controls tree size roughly like M.7, though in some trials trees were nearer M.26 size. It survived severe Polish test winters and resists collar rot, but is susceptible to fire blight and woolly aphid and is hard to propagate in stoolbeds. Little planted now; P 14 and P 60 are the Polish semi-dwarfs in current use.

name: P.2

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice
origin.note: From S.W. Zagaja's winter-hardiness breeding programme.

soil_notes: M.9-type requirements: fertile, weed-free soil with support and irrigation
best_for: M.9-sized intensive trees where M.9 suffers winter injury
avoid_when: fire-blight areas; tomato ringspot virus areas (Delicious on P.2 reacted like MM.106 in early Geneva tests)
notes: Polish M.9 x Antonovka dwarf giving trees about the size of M.9 (rated slightly smaller in some US sources). In Warsaw trials Elise on P 2 matched M.9 EMLA in size but yielded more; it is hardier in mid-winter than M.9 and fairly resistant to crown and root rots, with very few suckers. Susceptible to fire blight and woolly aphid.
